DiscoverStandard4–6 weeks

AI catalog enrichment with mandatory-field checks

Turn supplier sheets, pack photos and spec documents into complete, channel-ready listings. AI drafts titles, attributes and descriptions from approved facts, rules check mandatory declarations, and a category owner approves every listing before it goes live.

Fashion & apparel · FMCG & grocery · Beauty & personal care

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Listings are built by hand from supplier spreadsheets and pack photos, so attributes differ across Shopify, Amazon, Myntra and Nykaa, size charts go missing, and declarations such as net quantity, MRP, manufacturer or importer and country of origin are incomplete. Incomplete listings get suppressed by marketplaces and create avoidable complaints.

Trigger

A new SKU, supplier sheet or pack-artwork change is added to the product master sheet or PIM.

How it runs

  1. Collect the source data: supplier sheet, front and back pack photos, size chart or ingredient list, and documents such as the FSSAI license number.
  2. Extract label text and map it to each channel's attribute schema, flagging fields the source does not support instead of guessing.
  3. Check mandatory declarations: manufacturer, packer or importer, generic name, net quantity, MRP inclusive of taxes, country of origin and consumer care details, plus the FSSAI license number and label particulars for food.
  4. Draft titles, bullets and descriptions from approved facts only, and hold unsupported claims such as clinically proven, chemical-free or medicinal benefits for review.
  5. Send each draft to the category owner's approval queue with the source images side by side.
  6. Publish approved listings through channel APIs or each marketplace's bulk-upload template, update the Google Merchant Center and Meta catalog feeds, and log the approver and version.

Human checkpoint

The category or catalog manager approves every new or changed listing. Claims about cosmetics, food or nutrition go to the client's regulatory or legal reviewer before publishing.

DiscoverAdvanced5–8 weeks

Stock, price and batch sync across every sales channel

Keep sellable stock, prices and offers consistent across the D2C store, marketplaces and quick-commerce partners. Buffers prevent overselling, near-expiry batches are held back or proposed for markdown, and rate-linked prices such as gold jewelry are recalculated for approval.

FMCG & grocery · Electronics & appliances · Jewellery & luxury

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Stock lives in the warehouse system while each marketplace and quick-commerce partner holds its own count, so popular SKUs oversell and cancellations hurt seller ratings. Prices are uploaded by hand, discounts are announced without a traceable reference price, near-expiry batches ship late, and jewelry prices lag the daily metal rate.

Trigger

A stock movement in the OMS or WMS, a scheduled sync interval, a price or offer change approved in the pricing sheet, or the daily metal rate for jewelry.

How it runs

  1. Read sellable stock by location and batch from the OMS or WMS and subtract channel buffers agreed per SKU velocity.
  2. Exclude food batches that would reach the shopper with less shelf life than FSSAI's e-commerce advisory asks for, at least 30 percent or 45 days before expiry, and list them in a markdown proposal.
  3. For jewelry, recompute prices from net metal weight, the approved day rate, making charges, stone value and tax, and hold any change above the agreed tolerance.
  4. Keep a dated price history per SKU so any announced discount can show the prior price the amended E-Commerce Rules call for from January 1, 2027.
  5. Push stock and approved prices through channel APIs or partner upload files; for quick-commerce partners that buy on purchase orders, track open POs and listing content instead of pushing stock.
  6. Raise mismatches, API failures and oversell risks to the marketplace operations queue.

Human checkpoint

The pricing or marketplace manager approves price changes, markdown proposals and any jewelry price move beyond the tolerance. For jewelry, a named person confirms the day rate before it is used.

DiscoverStandard3–5 weeks

Creator collaboration and ad-disclosure workflow

Run creator and influencer programs from brief to repost with clear records: product seeding, approved claims sheets, disclosure checks, usage rights and sales by creator code. Built for beauty brands, where claims and disclosure draw close scrutiny.

Beauty & personal care

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Creator programs run on spreadsheets and DMs. Briefs drift from approved claims, paid or gifted posts miss disclosure labels, rights for reposting and ads are unclear, and nobody can tie a creator's content to orders. Beauty claims about skin results or natural and Ayurvedic positioning attract ASCI and regulatory attention.

Trigger

A creator is shortlisted for a campaign, or a creator submits draft content for review.

How it runs

  1. Record each creator's profile, agreed fee, past disclosures and consent to be contacted in the creator tracker.
  2. Generate the brief from an approved claims sheet that lists permitted wording and banned claims for each product.
  3. Track seeding shipments and agreed deliverables, and issue unique discount codes or UTM links.
  4. Pre-check draft captions and scripts with AI for the disclosure labels ASCI's influencer guidelines and the CCPA endorsement guidance expect, and for claims outside the approved sheet, then route them to a reviewer.
  5. Record usage rights and their expiry before any repost, whitelisting or paid amplification.
  6. Report orders, revenue and returns by creator code every week.

Human checkpoint

The brand manager approves every brief and final post. Claims about efficacy, skin conditions or ingredients go to the client's regulatory or legal reviewer; AI only flags issues.

EvaluateAdvanced5–7 weeks

Grounded fit, shade and spec advisor

Answer pre-purchase questions on size and fit, shade and skin type, or technical specs using only the brand's own size charts, shade guides, spec sheets and policies. When the answer is not in the approved sources, the assistant says so and hands over to a person.

Fashion & apparel · Electronics & appliances · Beauty & personal care

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Shoppers ask the same questions on WhatsApp and chat: will this fit, which shade suits me, does this inverter AC suit my room and power supply, is this charger compatible with my phone. Slow or inconsistent answers lose the sale and wrong answers create returns. Generic chatbots guess, which is worse.

Trigger

A shopper opens the size, shade or compare widget on a product page, or asks a product question on WhatsApp or web chat.

How it runs

  1. Index approved sources per category: garment measurements, fit notes and return reasons; shade charts and ingredient lists; spec sheets, compatibility tables and installation requirements.
  2. Capture the question and optional inputs through a short quiz, such as height and usual size, skin tone and type, or room size and power supply.
  3. Retrieve matching passages and draft an answer that cites its source and states uncertainty; nothing is answered from model memory.
  4. Give no medical or dermatological advice and no site-specific electrical-safety judgment, such as wiring or load suitability; route those questions to a trained person or the installation partner.
  5. Hand over to an agent with a summary when confidence is low, the shopper asks for a person, or the question concerns stock, price or delivery dates.
  6. Log unanswered questions as content gaps for the catalog team.

Human checkpoint

Category owners approve the knowledge sources and answer style before launch. Agents take over low-confidence, sensitive or out-of-scope conversations, and a reviewer samples transcripts every week.

Video and showroom consultation booking

Let shoppers book a video call or showroom visit with a designer or jewelry consultant, pass the right product context to the consultant beforehand, and send follow-ups, quotes and approved financing information after the call.

Home & furniture · Jewellery & luxury

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

High-value furniture and jewelry purchases need conversation, but inquiries arrive across Instagram, WhatsApp and calls and are answered late or lost. Consultants join calls without knowing what the shopper viewed, trade and interior-designer leads mix with retail ones, and EMI questions get improvised answers.

Trigger

A shopper clicks book a consultation on a product or collection page, replies to a click-to-WhatsApp ad, or submits a designer or trade inquiry form.

How it runs

  1. Offer open slots by consultant, language, store and category, and confirm by WhatsApp and calendar invite with a reschedule link.
  2. Attach the shopper's viewed products, wishlist, budget band and room or occasion notes to the consultant's brief.
  3. Route architects, interior designers and bulk buyers to the trade team with their own follow-up rules.
  4. Send a reminder before the call and a follow-up afterward with the shortlisted designs or quote.
  5. Answer EMI questions only with the current lender-approved terms text, and send the shopper to the lender or payment page for eligibility.
  6. Record outcomes such as quote sent, custom order or no sale in the CRM for follow-up.

Human checkpoint

Consultants own every quote, custom-design commitment and price exception. Financing eligibility is decided only by the lender, never by the automation.

Checkout and confirmStarter2–4 weeks

Consented cart and checkout recovery

Follow up abandoned carts only with shoppers who opted in, on the channel they chose, with honest messages: no fake countdowns, no pre-added items, the total price including fees shown upfront, and a clear way to opt out.

Beauty & personal care · Home & furniture

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Many carts are abandoned, but blanket WhatsApp and SMS reminders without opt-in risk blocks, paused templates and DND complaints. Urgency tricks such as fake stock counters, pre-added items or fees revealed late are dark patterns under the CCPA guidelines and erode trust.

Trigger

An identified shopper leaves checkout with items in the cart and holds an active marketing opt-in for email or WhatsApp.

How it runs

  1. Check consent and channel preference, suppression lists, recent purchases and open support tickets before anything is sent.
  2. After the agreed interval, send an approved WhatsApp marketing template or an email with the cart contents, the total price including delivery and COD fees, and the return policy link.
  3. For furniture, offer a consultation or delivery-date check instead of a discount; for beauty, offer shade or regimen help.
  4. Send no more than the agreed number of reminders, and stop at once on purchase, reply or opt-out.
  5. Route replies with questions to an agent inside the 24-hour customer service window.
  6. Report recovered revenue against a holdout group so the incremental effect is measured honestly.

Human checkpoint

The CRM or growth manager approves templates, frequency caps, any offer and the holdout design. The client's legal or compliance owner reviews message wording against the dark-pattern guidelines before launch.

Checkout and confirmStandard3–5 weeks

COD confirmation, address checks and high-value verification

Confirm cash-on-delivery orders on WhatsApp before dispatch, fix incomplete addresses, and hold risky or high-value orders for a person to review, so fewer parcels travel to doorsteps that will refuse them.

Fashion & apparel · Electronics & appliances · Jewellery & luxury

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Cash on delivery stays popular, and some COD orders are refused at the door, unreachable or placed with incomplete addresses. Each return to origin pays freight both ways and ties up stock; for fashion it often misses the season. Electronics and jewelry add fraud risk: high-value orders with mismatched details.

Trigger

A new order arrives in the storefront or OMS with COD payment, an address that fails validation, or a value above the high-value threshold.

How it runs

  1. Validate the address against the pincode serviceability master, flag missing house numbers or landmarks, and score risk from value, order history, pincode return history and past refusals.
  2. Send an approved WhatsApp utility template to shoppers who opted in to order updates at checkout, asking them to confirm the order and address, with buttons to confirm, edit the address or cancel.
  3. Where the client chooses, add an optional prepaid link. Any COD fee or prepaid benefit is shown at checkout, never added later, and no promotional incentive goes into the utility template.
  4. If WhatsApp is undelivered or the shopper has no WhatsApp opt-in, use a DLT-registered SMS service template or an IVR call, then hold the order for review.
  5. Queue high-risk and high-value orders with the evidence; for jewelry, collect any identity or PAN details the client's policy requires through a secure web form, not in chat.
  6. Release confirmed orders to the warehouse and log outcomes for return-to-origin analysis by pincode, channel and campaign.

Human checkpoint

An order-operations reviewer decides every held or high-value order: release, call the shopper or cancel. Cancellations the shopper asks for are processed as requested; the automation never cancels an order on its own.

DeliverStandard3–5 weeks

Proactive delivery updates and failed-delivery (NDR) resolution

Send the order updates shoppers actually need and act fast when a courier reports a failed delivery attempt: confirm the reason with the shopper, capture a new slot or corrected address, and send the reattempt instruction to the courier before cut-off.

Fashion & apparel · FMCG & grocery

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Courier NDR reasons such as customer not available or address incomplete are often unverified, and by the time support calls the shopper the parcel is already marked for return. Where-is-my-order messages flood support, and grocery and FMCG orders with short delivery windows cannot wait for a callback.

Trigger

A courier status event: shipped, out for delivery, delivery attempt failed (NDR), delayed beyond the promised date, or return to origin initiated.

How it runs

  1. Normalize courier status codes from the aggregator into one set of order states.
  2. Send utility-template updates at shipped and out for delivery to opted-in shoppers, with a tracking link and the courier contact, and DLT-registered SMS service messages to the rest.
  3. On an NDR event, send an approved template within minutes with the stated reason and options: reattempt tomorrow, choose a slot, update the address or landmark, or cancel.
  4. Send the shopper's choice to the courier's NDR action API, or the panel's bulk upload where no API exists, before the cut-off and confirm back to the shopper.
  5. Flag disputed reasons, such as a shopper saying no attempt was made, to the logistics team for escalation with the courier.
  6. For perishables and short-shelf-life items, hold reattempts that would breach the delivery window and pass the refund or reship decision to a person.

Human checkpoint

The logistics lead reviews disputed NDR reasons and courier escalations. A CX agent decides refunds or reships for perishable or delayed orders.

DeliverStandard4–6 weeks

Delivery slots, installation and warranty activation

Schedule delivery, installation, demo or assembly with the shopper and the service partner, capture serial numbers and photos at the visit, and activate the warranty automatically so later service starts from a verified record.

Electronics & appliances · Home & furniture

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Large appliances and furniture need a delivery slot, a technician or assembler and often a demo. Coordination happens on calls between the brand, courier and installation partner, so visits are missed, serial numbers are never captured, and warranty registration is left to shoppers, who rarely complete it.

Trigger

An order with an installable or assemble-on-site item ships, or the shopper requests a visit after delivery.

How it runs

  1. Offer delivery and installation or assembly slots by pincode, partner capacity and product type, and confirm on WhatsApp.
  2. Create a job for the service partner with product, address, slot and site needs such as wall type, power point or lift access.
  3. Send reminders with the technician or crew details on the day, with a reschedule option.
  4. At the visit, the technician records the serial number, installation photos and the shopper's sign-off in a mobile form.
  5. Validate the serial against the dispatch record, activate the warranty, or file it on the manufacturer's portal where the seller is not the brand, and send the warranty card and care guide.
  6. Escalate failed visits, damaged-on-arrival reports and serial mismatches to the service desk.

Human checkpoint

The service coordinator handles rescheduling conflicts, serial mismatches and damaged-on-arrival cases. Replacement and refund decisions stay with the brand's service manager.

Returns and supportStandard4–6 weeks

Returns, exchanges and damage claims with photo evidence

Let shoppers start a return, size exchange or damage claim in a few taps, check eligibility against the published policy, collect photos or unboxing video where needed, and route refunds and replacements to a person when evidence or value calls for it.

Fashion & apparel · Electronics & appliances · Home & furniture

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Returns arrive by email, WhatsApp and marketplace panels with missing photos and order numbers. Fashion teams lose sales an exchange could have saved, electronics teams struggle to judge damaged-on-arrival claims, and furniture transit-damage claims drag on while the customer waits.

Trigger

A shopper requests a return, exchange or damage claim from the order page, a WhatsApp message or a marketplace notification.

How it runs

  1. Look up the order and check eligibility against the published return window, category exclusions and condition rules.
  2. Offer an exchange for another size or color first where stock exists, and show refund options without pressure.
  3. Collect photos, unboxing video or serial-number images for damage and defect claims, and check they match the item ordered.
  4. Use AI to summarize the claim and flag mismatched or incomplete evidence for the reviewer, never to approve or reject.
  5. Book a reverse pickup or service visit, and issue the refund or replacement after the warehouse or technician check.
  6. Feed return reasons by SKU and size back to catalog and sizing owners.

Human checkpoint

A returns agent approves every refund or replacement outside the automatic rules, every damage and defect claim, and any high-value item. Disputed claims go to the CX lead.

Returns and supportAdvanced5–8 weeks

Policy-grounded support assistant with human handoff

Answer order, policy, product-care and service questions on WhatsApp and web chat from the store's own policies and live order data, raise service and quality tickets with the right details, and hand over to an agent whenever a question needs judgment.

FMCG & grocery · Electronics & appliances · Jewellery & luxury

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Support teams answer the same questions all day: where is my order, can I cancel, how do I use this, is this piece hallmarked, how do I claim warranty. Sale days overwhelm them and answers drift from the published policy. A bot that improvises refund or warranty terms creates disputes.

Trigger

A shopper messages the brand on WhatsApp, web chat or email.

How it runs

  1. Identify the shopper and order from the WhatsApp number or order ID, with a one-time code on web chat and email before sharing order details.
  2. Answer only from approved sources: return, cancellation, warranty and exchange policies, care guides, hallmark and HUID verification guidance, and live order status.
  3. For electronics, open a service ticket with model, serial number, purchase date and symptoms, and explain the visit or pickup process.
  4. For FMCG and grocery, capture the batch number and photos for quality or expiry complaints and route them to the quality team.
  5. Hand over to an agent with a summary when the shopper asks, confidence is low, or the topic is a refund dispute, safety issue, legal complaint or anything the policy does not cover.
  6. Acknowledge complaints within the grievance timelines the client publishes and track each to closure.

Human checkpoint

Agents own refunds, compensation, safety and quality complaints and every policy exception; the grievance officer handles escalated complaints. A QA reviewer samples conversations every week.

Replenishment, subscription and retailer reorder reminders

Remind consumers when a pack is likely to run out, run subscribe-and-save without traps, turn sample buyers into full-size customers, and let retailers and distributors reorder their usual basket on WhatsApp for a sales rep to confirm.

FMCG & grocery · Beauty & personal care

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Consumables are bought again on a predictable cycle, but brands send generic offers instead of a timely reminder, subscriptions are hard to pause or cancel, and sample buyers are never followed up. On the B2B side, kirana retailers and distributors reorder through calls and photos of handwritten lists that reps re-key.

Trigger

A shopper's estimated run-out date approaches, a subscription renewal is due, a sample was delivered, or a registered retailer sends a reorder message.

How it runs

  1. Estimate run-out per SKU from pack size, usage guidance and the shopper's own repeat interval.
  2. Send a reminder on the shopper's opted-in channel a few days before the estimate, with a one-tap reorder link.
  3. For subscriptions, send a renewal notice with skip, pause and cancel options as easy to use as subscribing was.
  4. For beauty sample buyers, follow up after the trial period with usage tips and a full-size option, never a pre-added item.
  5. For retailers who opted in, send the usual basket on an approved WhatsApp template, accept edits, apply the approved scheme and pass the draft order to the rep or distributor.
  6. Sync confirmed retailer orders to the DMS or ERP and confirm dispatch to the retailer.

Human checkpoint

The CRM manager approves reminder timing and offers. For retailer orders, the sales rep or distributor confirms credit limits, schemes and the final order before dispatch.

Reviews, drops, back-in-stock and lifecycle journeys

Use RFM segments and stated preferences to send the few messages shoppers value: review and photo requests after delivery, back-in-stock and new-drop alerts they signed up for, and reminders for occasions they chose to share, with reviews published unedited.

Fashion & apparel · Beauty & personal care · Jewellery & luxury

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Brands blast the whole list with every sale, which raises opt-outs and hurts WhatsApp quality ratings. Review requests go out before the parcel arrives or only to happy customers, back-in-stock sign-ups are never notified, and jewelry buyers who shared an anniversary date hear nothing until the next sale.

Trigger

Delivery is confirmed, a sold-out size or shade returns to stock, a new collection goes live, a segment changes, or a saved occasion date approaches.

How it runs

  1. Build RFM and preference segments in the warehouse from orders, returns and stated preferences such as size, shade or metal.
  2. Request a review and photo from every buyer a set time after delivery, not only satisfied ones, and publish reviews without changing their meaning.
  3. Notify back-in-stock sign-ups in sign-up order when the exact size or shade returns.
  4. Send new-drop previews to opted-in segments with the real stock position and no fake scarcity.
  5. Send occasion reminders only to buyers who saved the date for that purpose, with an easy way to remove it.
  6. Measure each journey against a holdout and retire messages that do not earn their place.

Human checkpoint

The CRM manager approves segments, frequency caps and copy. A moderator reviews flagged reviews under a published moderation policy, guided by the voluntary BIS standard IS 19000:2022, and never removes a review for being negative.
